**merge** two sorted halves into one sorted array: $\Theta(n)$.

Split in half, sort each half, merge. But how do the halves get sorted?

::: notes
Recap from Wednesday. Merge walks a finger along each half and copies the
smaller item each time; every item is copied once, so it's linear.

The question we left hanging: the halves. Answer: the same way. Sort each
half by splitting it in half…
:::

## mergeSort {.smaller .smallcode}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="45%"}
1. If the array has 0 or 1 elements, it's sorted.
2. Split the array into halves.
3. Sort each half recursively.
4. Merge the two halves.
:::
::: {.column width="55%"}
```cpp
void mergeSort(vector<T> & A, int lo, int hi) {
    if (hi > lo) {
        int mid = (hi + lo)/2;
        mergeSort(A, lo, mid);
        mergeSort(A, mid+1, hi);
        merge(A, lo, mid, hi);
    }
}
```
:::
::::

RT:

::: notes
Write the recurrence beside RT. With $T(n)$ the time to sort $n$ items:

$$T(1) = b, \qquad T(n) = 2\,T(n/2) + cn$$

Two recursive calls on half the input, plus a linear merge. The split itself
is constant. Assume $n$ is a power of 2 so the halves are exact.
:::

## Closed form 1: expand and generalize {.smaller}

$T(n) = 2\,T(n/2) + cn, \quad T(1) = b$

::: notes
$$
\begin{aligned}
T(n) &= 2T(n/2) + cn \\
     &= 4T(n/4) + 2cn \\
     &= 8T(n/8) + 3cn \\
     &\;\;\vdots \\
     &= 2^k\,T(n/2^k) + kcn
\end{aligned}
$$

The base case is reached when $n/2^k = 1$, i.e. $k = \log n$:

$$T(n) = n\,T(1) + cn\log n = cn\log n + bn.$$
:::

::: notes
Each level does a total of $cn$ work: one $n$, two $n/2$'s, four $n/4$'s…
The leaves are $n$ base cases at $b$ each.

The tree has $\log n$ levels of merging, so the total is
$cn\log n + bn$ — the same answer as expanding.
:::

## Proving the closed form is correct: {.smaller}

**Thm:** $\forall n \ge 1,\; T(n) \le cn\log n + bn.$

::: notes
By induction on $n$ (powers of 2).

**Base case**, $n = 1$: $T(1) = b \le c \cdot 1 \cdot 0 + b \cdot 1 = b$. ✓

**IH:** assume $T(j) \le cj\log j + bj$ for all $j < n$.

**Inductive step**, $n > 1$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
T(n) &= 2T(n/2) + cn \\
     &\le 2\left(c\tfrac{n}{2}\log\tfrac{n}{2} + b\tfrac{n}{2}\right) + cn \\
     &= cn(\log n - 1) + bn + cn \\
     &= cn\log n + bn.
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

## MergeSort correctness: {.smaller .proof}

Call mergeSort: `mergeSort(A, 0, A.size()-1);`

```cpp
void mergeSort(vector<T> & A, int lo, int hi) {
    if (hi > lo) {
        int mid = (hi + lo)/2;
        mergeSort(A, lo, mid);
        mergeSort(A, mid+1, hi);
        merge(A, lo, mid, hi);
    }
}
```

Claim: `mergeSort` correctly sorts `A[lo..hi]` for any `(hi-lo+1)` \_\_\_\_\_\_\_\_

Let $n$ = `(hi - lo + 1)`, arbitrary.

$n \le 1$: (Base Case)

$n > 1$: IH: Assume `mergeSort` correctly sorts a slice of size $j$, for any $j < n$.

`int mid = (hi + lo)/2;`

`mergeSort(A, lo, mid);` <br> `mergeSort(A, mid+1, hi);`

::: notes
The blank: **$\ge 0$**. The empty slice counts.

**Base case**, $n \le 1$: `hi > lo` is false, nothing happens, and a slice
of 0 or 1 items is already sorted.

**$n > 1$:** because `lo < hi`, `mid` satisfies `lo ≤ mid < hi`. Why:

- **lo ≤ mid:** the average of lo and something at least lo is at least
  lo, and rounding down can't take it below lo, because lo is a whole
  number.
- **mid < hi:** since lo ≤ hi − 1, the average is at most hi − ½, and
  rounding down keeps it below hi.

It only works because lo < hi, which is why the 0-or-1 case has to be the
base case: with lo = hi, mid = hi and the first call would be the same call
again.

So both
`A[lo..mid]` and `A[mid+1..hi]` have at least one item and **fewer than
$n$**. That's exactly what the IH needs: both recursive calls sort their
halves.
:::

## MergeSort correctness, continued: {.smaller}

`merge(A, lo, mid, hi);`

\

Conclusion:

\

\

**To contemplate:**

- does the value of `mid` matter in the correctness proof?
- does the value of `mid` matter in the analysis of the runtime?
- could we do a $k$-way merge sort?

::: notes
`merge` takes two sorted slices that sit side by side and produces one
sorted slice of the same items. (Its own correctness is a loop invariant:
the output so far is sorted and holds the smallest items seen.)

**Conclusion:** `A[lo..hi]` is sorted. Since $n$ was arbitrary,
`mergeSort` sorts every slice, and in particular the call
`mergeSort(A, 0, A.size()-1)` sorts the whole array.

To contemplate:

- **Correctness:** no. Any `mid` with `lo ≤ mid < hi` works — the proof
  only needs both halves to be smaller.
- **Runtime:** yes. Split off one item at a time (`mid = lo`) and the
  recurrence becomes $T(n) = T(n-1) + cn$, which is $\Theta(n^2)$.
- **$k$-way:** yes. $\log_k n$ levels, but each merge now picks the
  smallest of $k$ fronts. Still $\Theta(n \log n)$.
:::

## Where are we in the sorting picture? {.smaller}

| | Best case | Worst case |
|---|:---:|:---:|
| **Insertion** | $O(n)$ | $O(n^2)$ |
| **Selection** | $O(n^2)$ | $O(n^2)$ |
| **Merge** | $O(n\log n)$ | $O(n\log n)$ |

\

Watch them race: <https://visualgo.net/en/sorting>

::: notes
Merge sort doesn't care about the input order, like selection sort — but it
sits at $n \log n$ instead of $n^2$.

Next: is $n \log n$ the best a comparison sort can do?
:::
